prompt.context: Your client is a cell phone carrier in Western Europe in the late 1990s when growth is exploding. The market as a whole is approximately 60% penetrated. Your client is concerned because acquisition costs (the cost to acquire a new customer) have been increasing at a 20% CAGR over the past few years.
prompt.question: Your client wants to know why acquisition costs are increasing and what they should do.

clarifying_info.q: What are the main components of acquisition costs?
clarifying_info.a: Acquisition costs largely fall into two categories: (1) handset subsidies — phones are given to customers for free, and (2) commissions to independent stores who sell the phones.

clarifying_info.q: What is the total annual acquisition cost per customer?
clarifying_info.a: Total annual acquisition costs are 200 euros per customer.

clarifying_info.q: How much of the total acquisition cost is attributable to handset subsidies, and how fast have handset costs been growing?
clarifying_info.a: Total handset spending is 100 euros per customer, but handsets only account for 5% CAGR of the total increase. The remainder of growth comes from commissions.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have other distribution outlets besides independent stores? Are stores equally distributed geographically?
clarifying_info.a: No — the stores are not equally distributed geographically.

clarifying_info.q: How does the commission structure work — are there different rates for different plans?
clarifying_info.a: Assume only one plan for simplicity. All commissions are paid against that plan. Commissions represent the entire increase in acquisition costs; there are no other marketing expenses. Plan prices have been consistent over time, so that is not driving the increase.

clarifying_info.q: Have competitors changed — more entrants, differentiated plans, different distribution?
clarifying_info.a: Competitors have been consistent over time, though competition is increasing. Market share is consistent across players; plans are non-differentiated. Competitors use similar distribution channels — in fact the same stores. Commissions across the industry have been increasing at a similar rate.

clarifying_info.q: Have customer purchasing habits changed — where they buy, preference for certain plans or phones?
clarifying_info.a: Customers are buying through the same channels as always; client plans and phones are competitive.

clarifying_info.q: Do the independent stores also sell competitors' phones?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, they do. That is why the client has to incentivize them so well.

framework: Identify the primary drivers of the increase in acquisition costs by decomposing total acquisition cost into its components (handset subsidies and store commissions) and determining how much each component has been growing
Quantify the growth split: handsets growing at ~5% CAGR, commissions growing much faster (~35% CAGR) and are the dominant driver

Explore why commissions are rising: investigate the competitive dynamics of the distribution channel, noting that independent stores sell all carriers' phones and therefore require increasing incentives to push any one carrier
Benchmark the client's cost structure and commission levels against competitors to identify whether more cost-effective strategies exist
Develop options to reduce acquisition costs, focusing on the fastest-growing and most significant cost element (commissions)

questions.prompt: Given that total acquisition costs are growing at 20% CAGR and handsets (100 euros of the 200 euro total) are only contributing 5% CAGR to that growth, what is the implied CAGR of commissions?
questions.guidance: A strong answer correctly attributes the residual growth to commissions. Since handsets account for 50% of spend but only 5% CAGR, commissions must be growing at roughly 35% CAGR to produce the blended 20% overall growth. Candidate should set up the weighted-average equation and solve.

math.setup: Total cost = 200 euros. Handsets = 100 euros (50% of total), growing at 5% CAGR. Commissions = 100 euros (50% of total), growing at X% CAGR. Blended CAGR = 0.5 * 5% + 0.5 * X% = 20%.
math.answer: Commissions are growing at approximately 35% CAGR.

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of the escalating commissions?
questions.guidance: The key insight is that independent stores serve as a shared distribution channel selling phones for all carriers simultaneously. Because stores can steer customers toward any carrier, each carrier must keep raising commissions to maintain store preference. This is a classic multi-principal agent problem / commission bidding war in a shared channel. The interviewer's clue that competitors use 'similar distribution channels — down to the same store' is critical.

questions.prompt: What options does the client have to reduce or control acquisition costs?
questions.guidance: A strong answer generates several distinct levers: (1) signal the market that escalating commissions will stop (PR / industry coordination); (2) differentiate product offerings (plan features, handset selection) so stores have reason to recommend the client without extra incentive; (3) shift marketing spend toward consumer pull (advertising, brand) to reduce dependence on store-level push; (4) develop alternative, lower-cost distribution channels such as the internet, company-owned stores, or direct sales to reduce reliance on the shared independent store network.

brainstorming.prompt: What actions could the client take to control or reduce rising acquisition costs?

categories.name: Channel strategy
ideas: Establish proprietary distribution (company-owned stores, website, direct sales)
Reduce dependence on independent stores that sell all competitors

categories.name: Product differentiation
ideas: Differentiate plan offerings to create consumer pull and reduce need to outbid competitors for store promotion
Offer exclusive or superior handsets to draw customers in independently

categories.name: Marketing and demand generation
ideas: Increase consumer-directed advertising so customers arrive at the store already decided, reducing the store's influence
Build brand loyalty programs to retain customers and lower re-acquisition need

categories.name: Commission structure reform
ideas: Signal market-wide intent to cap commissions via industry body or PR
Shift from pure volume commissions to performance-based or tiered structures
Negotiate exclusivity or preferred-placement arrangements with high-traffic stores

recommendation: The primary driver of rising acquisition costs is escalating commissions to independent stores, which are growing at ~35% CAGR — not handset subsidies. The root cause is a shared distribution channel where stores sell all carriers' phones, creating a bidding war for store attention.

The client should pursue a dual strategy: (1) invest in alternative, proprietary distribution channels (internet, owned stores) to reduce dependence on shared independents, and (2) differentiate product offerings and build consumer pull through marketing to reduce the leverage independent stores hold.
risks: Building proprietary channels requires upfront capital and time; commissions will continue rising in the interim
Differentiation is difficult in a commodity market where plans and handsets are non-differentiated across carriers
Signaling a commission cap could backfire if competitors do not follow, causing the client to lose shelf space
next_steps: Quantify the cost and timeline for establishing an internet or direct sales channel
Conduct customer research to identify plan or handset features that could meaningfully differentiate the offer
Model the break-even point at which proprietary channel investment pays back versus continued commission escalation
